Notion’s core servers were never breached.

Yet on November 12, Notion warned enterprise customers to immediately rotate every password, API key, and secret ever pasted into Notion AI.

How does your company’s sensitive data get exposed when your vendor’s infrastructure remains intact?

Welcome to the fourth-party AI inference trap.

To power its "Insights" feature with open-weight models, Notion routed prompts to an external inference provider: Fireworks AI. When attackers breached Fireworks AI to harvest LLM tokens, they walked away with Notion AI customer chat transcripts. Notion quickly severed the connection and disabled Insights.

Three days prior, on November 9, NEAR AI disclosed a similar hit. Attackers exploited a Remote Code Execution flaw in SGLang (CERT/CC VU#281278), bypassing Confidential Computing enclaves from the inside to intercept live prompts and steal cloud API keys from logs.

For the C-Suite, the reality is brutal: your AI supply chain is deeper than your vendor contracts admit.

When engineers paste `.env` credentials or executives summarize M&A strategy inside a SaaS AI assistant, that prompt leaves your tenant via API to an external GPU sub-processor.

In Indonesia, the clock on this blind spot is ticking.

On January 16, 2027, PP 33/2026 takes full effect under the PDP Law. You remain the legal Data Controller. Blaming a SaaS vendor's fourth-party GPU provider will not shield your balance sheet.

Under Articles 74 and 120, high-risk AI requires a DPIA and a granular Record of Processing Activities. If your ROPA stops at "Notion" and misses "Fireworks AI," your compliance posture is already broken.

Then comes the 72-hour trap under Articles 114 and 115. You have strictly 3x24 hours, including weekends, to report a breach. Look at the timeline: Fireworks detected access on Nov 2, confirmed impact to Notion on Nov 6, and Notion notified users on Nov 9. By the time a fourth-party breach reaches your inbox, your statutory 72-hour window is already dead—exposing your P&L to fines up to 2% of annual revenue and public naming.

Put your General Counsel and CISO in the same room this week and ask:

"Have we mapped the GPU inference sub-processors behind every AI-enabled SaaS tool we use, and does our SLA legally force them to notify us within 24 hours of a fourth-party breach?"

These are my personal opinions, shared from a genuine passion for education and research in cybersecurity. They do not represent the views of my employer.

Dhaka to host 51st ICQCC from November 18
Dhaka Tribune Report

The 51st International Convention on Quality Control Circles (ICQCC-2026) will be held in Dhaka from November 18 to 20 under the theme “QCC for Sustainable Development.”

The Bangladesh Society for Total Quality Management (BSTQM) and the University of Asia Pacific (UAP) are jointly organizing the convention. Around 8,000 members of approximately 800 Quality Control Circle (QCC) teams from 16 countries and regions are expected to participate.

Details of the convention were shared at a press conference held at Pan Pacific Sonargaon Dhaka on Sunday.
Those present included BSTQM President and ICQCC-2026 Convener A K M Shamsul Huda, BSTQM Adviser Engr. A M M Khairul Bashar, UAP Registrar Brig Gen (Retd) Prof Dr A K M Nazrul Islam, BSTQM Secretary General M M Kabir, and ICQCC-2026 Technical and Evaluation Committee Member Md Rokibul Islam, along with representatives of BSTQM and UAP and members of the media.

Of the participating teams, 141 will present onsite and 652 online. The main presentation sessions will be held at UAP on November 19 and 20, where teams will showcase workplace improvement projects focusing on productivity, quality enhancement, cost reduction and problem-solving.

Nearly 100 local and international judges will evaluate the presentations.

Participating countries and regions include Japan, China, India, South Korea, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Sri Lanka, the Philippines, Taiwan, Namibia, Zambia, Mozambique and Mauritius, along with Bangladesh.

ICQCC is coordinated internationally by the Union of Japanese Scientists and Engineers (JUSE) of Japan and is known as the “Quality Olympics.” It is one of the world's largest annual platforms for promoting QCC and Total Quality Management (TQM).
Bangladesh is hosting the convention for the third time.

The convention will conclude on November 20 with the announcement of results, a prize-giving ceremony and the formal handover of the ICQCC flag to the Philippines, host of the next convention.

Renting GPUs in a third-country data center used to sit largely outside US export rules. As of this week's rule, it doesn't.

The US Commerce Department's BIS: the remote access rule.

On Monday BIS released a 132-page interim final rule (IFR) aimed at one loophole: companies headquartered in China training frontier models on US chips by renting compute in data centers abroad. According to law firm Dorsey & Whitney, BIS is ending a longstanding interpretation that treated remote access to hardware as largely outside the EAR.

What the rule says:
• Threshold: data centers (single or "linked") offering more than 12,000,000 aggregate TPP (total processing performance)
• Scope: customers headquartered, or whose ultimate parent is headquartered, in Country Group D:5 (China plus 21 other locations) or Macau; applies to data centers worldwide
• New license requirement for advanced chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, 5 countries with a "higher-than-normal risk of diversion"
• Timeline: effective on Federal Register publication; 60-day comment period; data centers already serving these customers have 90 days to get a license
• The Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule is formally rescinded
• Carve-out: commercial recommender systems used by online retailers and social media

The detail that stands out to me: per Dorsey, if a supplier cannot verify a foreign data center's compliance, BIS may deem the supplier to have "knowledge". The question is no longer "who did I sell the chip to?" but "whose model is my chip training?"

What this means in practice:
1. Neoclouds and colocation providers need ultimate-parent ownership checks on every large customer.
2. Chip and server distributors should expect new contract clauses and compliance attestations.
3. If you rent overseas GPUs for training, budget time for new KYC-style paperwork.

My take as an AI engineer: export control has moved from the chip in the box to the compute behind the API. A GPU-hour is now a strategic good.

Will restricting compute access slow the rise of open-weight models, or accelerate it?

MINI PILE CONSTRUCTION: MORE THAN JUST INSTALLING PILES INTO THE GROUND

Looking back at my experience as a Geotechnical Engineer at PT. Frankipile Indonesia in 2017, working in the specialist foundation construction industry taught me an important lesson: successful foundation work is not simply about installing piles into the ground. It is about understanding how the ground behaves and ensuring that the foundation performs as intended.

Mini pile construction may look straightforward from the outside, but there are several engineering considerations behind every installation.

From a geotechnical engineering perspective, I believe there are five important aspects that deserve attention:

1. Understanding the Ground Conditions

Every foundation starts with understanding the soil. Geotechnical investigation, borehole logs, SPT values, groundwater conditions, and soil stratification provide the basis for determining the appropriate foundation system.

A pile length that works well in one location does not necessarily deliver the same performance somewhere else, even within the same project site.

2. Selecting the Right Installation Method

Whether using impact driving or hydraulic press-in methods, equipment selection must consider soil conditions, site restrictions, nearby structures, and construction requirements.

The objective is not simply to achieve the required penetration, but to install the pile without compromising its structural integrity or the surrounding ground conditions.

3. Controlling Pile Installation Quality

Pile positioning, verticality, penetration depth, driving resistance, and pile joint connections are important parameters that require proper supervision.

A small deviation during installation can potentially affect the load distribution and overall performance of the foundation system.

4. Verifying Foundation Performance

Installation records alone cannot tell the entire story. Appropriate verification through static load testing, dynamic load testing (PDA), and other relevant inspections helps establish whether the installed foundation meets the design requirements.

This is where geotechnical engineering meets actual field performance.

5. Looking Beyond Individual Pile Capacity

A foundation does not work as an individual pile alone. Pile group interaction, settlement, lateral resistance, pile cap connections, and structural load transfer must be considered as one integrated system.

One lesson I still carry from my experience in foundation construction:

We should never judge the quality of piling work merely by how many piles have been installed or how quickly the work has been completed.

Should Southeast Asia build its own military drones? Yes, but not from a blank sheet. Four wars say the advantage sits in components, software and how fast you can change them. Build the loop. Buy the airframe.

What did Malaysia buy? In June 2026 the Royal Malaysian Air Force launched No. 11 Squadron at Labuan with three imported medium-altitude long-endurance drones, contracted in 2023 for RM423.8 million, about US$100 million, with ground control and two years of training. At the US$300 to US$400 Ukraine pays for a strike drone, that sum buys more than 250,000. The comparison is unfair, but it shows how the region still thinks in airframes. Nothing public says how much of that money stayed in Malaysia, or what Malaysian engineers may change once support ends.

How did Ukraine scale? Its forces received about 3 million FPV drones in 2025, close to 2.5 times the year before, mostly made at home, with more than 7 million unmanned systems planned for 2026. Yet 97 percent of Ukrainian drone producers named China as a primary import source, and Chinese suppliers made up about 89 percent of drone-related imports by value in the first half of 2024. Ukraine won on integration and iteration, not on parts.

Is the US doing better? The Pentagon's Drone Dominance program targets 300,000 one-way attack drones. By June 2026 it had ordered 20,000 and accepted 1,040.

Can anyone build without China? Taiwan makes about 15,000 drones a month and still pays two to three times the Chinese price.

What should ASEAN own? Systems integration, payloads, secure data links and anti-jam navigation, ground control and mission software, counter-drone, training and maintenance. Airframes can be licensed, under contracts that grant firmware access, local upgrade rights and maintenance without the manufacturer's permission after warranty. Malaysia's National Defence Industry Policy of 21 January 2026 points the right way: a 30 percent local content floor and local MRO once warranties expire.

For the defense industry, the contract is now the capability. Transfer scope, firmware rights, component origin and modification cycle time are the terms LRY Group and Cavalier Nexus work through with defense manufacturers and the forces they supply.

ASEAN is encouraging partnerships to make AI tools, cloud services and training more accessible to micro, small and medium enterprises.

The focus includes women-led businesses, rural communities and programmes in local languages.

For business owners, the potential benefits are straightforward: less paperwork, faster customer service and more time to run the business.

Training, reliable connectivity and data protection are part of the commitment. Getting businesses to use AI properly matters as much as getting them to use it.

2. More regional opportunities for digital talent

ASEAN will explore ways to help skilled digital professionals work across the region, including voluntary pilot programmes and better comparability and recognition of qualifications.

Businesses could gain access to a wider talent pool. Workers could have more options to find opportunities matching their skills.

This is still being developed. Each country retains control over its immigration rules, work permits and employment requirements.

But it gives the region a starting point to address skills shortages together.

3. Space cooperation with practical benefits

The declaration supports sharing Earth observation data for disaster response, satellite ground infrastructure, joint research and technical training.

For countries regularly hit by floods and typhoons, better information and coordination could help authorities respond faster.

It also supports regional space businesses and technology transfer. ASEAN will develop a cooperation roadmap with measurable targets and timelines.

There are opportunities here for local companies, universities, researchers and engineers.

These three areas fit together.

Small businesses need affordable tools. Companies need skilled people. Countries can share infrastructure and expertise where it makes sense.

The Philippines deserves credit for advancing these commitments during its ASEAN chairmanship.

The next test is delivery: useful AI support that small businesses can access, talent mobility pilots that work, and space cooperation that produces practical results.

There’s plenty to be positive about if ASEAN follows through. More reasons for our businesses to grow, our people to build their careers here, and our countries to work together.

An engineering concept you can walk through.
From drawings to an interactive digital twin, right in the browser. 🌊
I built an interactive, browser-based digital twin of an FPSO and its unmanned wellhead platform using indicative pre-FEED parameters representative of real offshore conditions.
Engineering scope
• FPSO: LOA ~205 m, beam ~41 m, draft ~15.5 m, displacement ~122,000 t.
• Topsides: inlet separation, produced-water treatment, TEG dehydration, dew-point control, gas compression and metering.
• Utilities: 3 × GTG (N+1), WHRU and EDG.
• Subsea: production flowline, umbilical, lazy-wave riser and gas export tie-in.
• Marine: 4 × 3 spread mooring, tandem offloading, floating hose and ASD tug support.
• WHP: unmanned, multi-level decks, Christmas trees, production/test headers and pig launcher.
• Safety: 500 m zones, pipeline corridor, crane limits, helideck sectors, flare radiation and escape routes.
Interactive operations
Sea states from 0–8 m Hs drive operating limits. Crane work, helicopter operations, offloading, WHP visits and open-deck activities automatically shift between GO, CAUTION and STOP.
Development approach
Built iteratively with Claude as an engineering co-pilot—not from a single prompt. I refined layouts against reference drawings, corrected equipment logic, added marine and safety layers, and tested walk mode, sea states and operating scenarios.
AI accelerated the process; engineering judgement, design assumptions and validation remained essential.
The goal is to help engineers, operators and management understand the facility, hazards and operating envelope before FEED.
Indicative pre-FEED concept. Names anonymised; values indicative. Not a project design document.

The 51st International Convention on Quality Control Circles (ICQCC-2026) will be held in Dhaka from November 18 to 20 under the theme “QCC for Sustainable Development”.

Bangladesh Society for Total Quality Management (BSTQM) and the University of Asia Pacific (UAP) will jointly organise the convention, which is expected to bring together approximately 800 Quality Control Circle (QCC) teams and around 8,000 QCC members from 16 countries and regions.

The briefing was attended by BSTQM President and ICQCC-2026 Convener A K M Shamsul Huda, BSTQM Adviser Engr A M M Khairul Bashar, UAP Registrar Brig Gen (Retd) Prof Dr A K M Nazrul Islam, BSTQM Secretary General M M Kabir, ICQCC-2026 Technical and Evaluation Committee Member Md Rokibul Islam, representatives of BSTQM and UAP, and media representatives.

Of the participating teams, 141 will make their presentations onsite, while 652 will participate online. The main presentation sessions will take place on November 19 and 20 at UAP, where the teams will present workplace improvement projects focusing on productivity, quality enhancement, cost reduction and problem-solving.

Participating countries and regions include Japan, China, India, South Korea, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Sri Lanka, the Philippines, Taiwan, Namibia, Zambia, Mozambique and Mauritius, along with Bangladesh.

Internationally coordinated by JUSE (Union of Japanese Scientists and Engineers), Japan, ICQCC is widely known as the “Quality Olympics” and is one of the world's largest annual platforms for promoting Quality Control Circles (QCC) and Total Quality Management (TQM).

Bangladesh is hosting the convention for the third time.

External Shocks Expose Internal Fragility
Market volatility rarely creates weaknesses in a business; more often, it reveals existing ones.

For Indonesian leaders, external pressure arrives from multiple directions. Karhutla can disrupt supply chains, regulatory shifts can demand sudden adjustments, and tighter financing can pressure liquidity.

The challenge is not merely managing each disruption. It is keeping operations moving, serving customers, and deciding what comes next.

In conversations with leadership teams, one pattern stands out: disruption comes from outside, yet operational paralysis happens inside. A compliance update or supply delay can stall execution, not because teams lack capability, but because too many adjustments still need the founder's intervention.

External volatility is a business reality. Institutional resilience is an organizational choice.

In a Hero-Mode organization, pressure exposes how much still depends on individual intervention. Risk ownership is unclear, contingencies live in personal memory rather than documented practice, and decisions stay at the top.

A business built this way performs under familiar conditions but struggles when conditions shift. Management attention moves from strategy to firefighting, delivery becomes less predictable, and margins come under pressure.

Institutional partners and lenders look beyond financial statements to assess whether the organization can maintain operational control under pressure.

Moving to Architect-Mode is not about eliminating uncertainty. It is about building response capacity: clear risk ownership, scenario planning, documented contingencies, and decision rights distributed to execution leads.

You cannot choose the environment you operate in, but you can build an organization that keeps its footing when that environment changes.

Resilience is not measured by how much pressure a founder can absorb. It is measured by whether the organization can continue making sound decisions when pressure arrives. 

And when tested, what gives an investor confidence that it remains in control?

Back in June, I was fortunate to travel to Bandung as an Australian delegate for the CAUSINDY — Conference of Australian and Indonesian Youth 2026. Across four days, we toured the 192 MWp Cirata Floating Solar Plant, visited the KONEKSI EV battery project, and worked alongside Indonesian engineers, researchers, and policymakers.
 
Coming from the Australian clean energy sector, seeing Indonesia’s energy transition up close was eye-opening. A few key takeaways that stuck with me:

The subsidy trap: As a net oil importer, Indonesia heavily subsidises transport fuels while capping domestic coal prices for power generation. That keeps grid tariffs artificially low - putting commercial solar right around grid parity - while leaving the state budget carrying billions in utility subsidies.

The EV supply chain paradox: While EV adoption on Indonesian roads is tiny, Indonesia supplies over 60% of the world’s mined nickel - accounting for 60–80% of the nickel used in long-range EVs globally. Banning raw ore exports successfully forced domestic refining investment, yet much of that processing runs on off-grid "captive" coal plants - baking heavy embodied carbon into the global EV transition.

Floating PV is a serious solution: Seeing floating solar firsthand - and hearing from industry experts - highlighted how viable floating solar is across Indonesia’s calm inland seas and hydro reservoirs. It sidesteps land constraints, cuts evaporation, and plugs straight into existing hydro transmission infrastructure.
 
Grateful to CAUSINDY, KINETIK, and our hosts in Bandung for pulling together a great week—good to step outside the Australian bubble and see how another grid operates firsthand.

The 51st International Convention on Quality Control Circles (ICQCC-2026) will be held in Dhaka from 18 to 20 November under the theme “QCC for Sustainable Development.”

Details of the convention were shared at a press conference held at Pan Pacific Sonargaon Dhaka. The briefing was attended by Engr. A.M.M. khairul Bashar, Adviser of BSTQM; AKM Shamsul Huda, President of BSTQM and Convener of ICQCC-2026; Brig. Gen. (Retd.) Prof. Dr. A K M Nazrul Islam, Registrar of the University of Asia Pacific (UAP); M M Kabir, Secretary General of BSTQM; Prof. Dr. A F M Nazmus Sadat, Joint Secretary of BSTQM; Md. Rokibul Islam, Member of the Technical and Evaluation Committee of ICQCC-2026; representatives of BSTQM and UAP; and members of the media.

Jointly organized by the Bangladesh Society for Total Quality Management (BSTQM) and the University of Asia Pacific (UAP), the convention is expected to bring together approximately 800 Quality Control Circle (QCC) teams and around 8,000 QCC members from 16 countries and regions.

Among the participating teams, 141 will present onsite and 652 online. The main presentation sessions will be held on 19 and 20 November at UAP, where teams will showcase workplace improvement projects focusing on productivity enhancement, quality improvement, cost reduction, and problem-solving. Nearly 100 local and international judges will evaluate the presentations.

Participating countries include Japan, China, India, South Korea, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Sri Lanka, the Philippines, Taiwan, Namibia, Zambia, Mozambique, and Mauritius, along with Bangladesh.

Coordinated internationally by the Union of Japanese Scientists and Engineers (JUSE), ICQCC is widely recognized as the “Quality Olympics.” It is one of the world's largest annual international platforms for promoting Quality Control Circles (QCC) and Total Quality Management (TQM). Hosted in rotation among ICQCC member countries, the convention is being held in Bangladesh for the third time.

Speaking at the press conference, A K M Shamsul Huda said, “Hosting this international convention in Bangladesh for the third time is a significant milestone for the country's quality movement. It provides an excellent opportunity to showcase Bangladesh's capabilities, achievements and hospitality to the global community.”

The convention will conclude on 20 November with the announcement of results, a prize-giving ceremony, and the formal handover of the ICQCC flag to the Philippines, host of the next convention.

Better rainfall forecasts only save lives when they reach the people who need them.

On October 21, 2026, Weathernews Inc. andIndonesian Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics (BMKG) signed a Collaboration Agreement at BMKG's Multi Hazard Early Warning System (MHEWS) building in Jakarta. The theme: jointly strengthening rainfall forecasting and communicating it to the public.

🤝 What we will build together
・Co-development of an AI-based rainfall prediction system, planned over three years
・Combining BMKG's historical and real-time radar data with WNI's AI modeling expertise
・Technical guidance, capacity building for BMKG staff, and evaluation and operational management of the system
・A phased approach: weather radar data first, then other observation data after evaluation

🌍 Looking ahead
・The target is to release the results to the public in the 2027–2028 rainy season
・Both sides emphasized going beyond nowcasting toward outputs with measurable operational value
・We plan to hold a Technical Workshop, mainly with engineers from NVIDIA, BMKG and WNI, to discuss best practices for using AI models

BMKG's Executive Secretary, Mr. Guswanto, described the agreement as a strategic step aligned with the UN's Early Warnings for All (EW4All) initiative and the WMO Strategic Plan 2024–2027.

This is a new initiative that builds on our ongoing "AI-based Cyclone & Flood Forecast" project. We are grateful to BMKG for their trust, and we look forward to working together to turn forecasts into action.

Together, under the same sky.

posts.text:
Bank's VP: "Here in the U.S., you can be anything you want to be."
Me: “Ma’am, if you take a look at my CV I already became someone I wanted to be, even in Indonesia. Progress has been made, you can read it in my CV.”
Bank's VP: (immediately glanced back at computer screen and awkward silence atmosphere followed).
 
Many candidates like me, with 20+ years of three global companies, a global client, and local-pride organizations, are not trying to "be somebody" anymore.
We have already built careers, led teams, supported organizations, solved problems, and delivered results. We are not seeking validation through a title. We are seeking an opportunity to continue contributing at a level we have already earned.
This is where I believe the human side of recruiting matters more than ever.

AI can make recruiting faster. It can summarize resumes, identify keywords, rank applicants, and streamline screening. These are valuable tools.
But AI should help recruiters prepare for conversations, not replace genuine curiosity and attentive listening.
Reading a candidate's CV before the interview is not merely preparation. It is a sign of respect for the time, effort, and experience the candidate brings to the table, what have been done and what have been accomplished.

A conversation reveals the depth behind those accomplishments.
Before asking candidates who they want to become, it may be worth understanding who they have already become through decades of experience, resilience, and contribution.
The best hiring decisions happen when technology and human judgment work together, not when one replaces the other.
AI can identify a candidate. Only attentive recruiters can truly understand one.
 
On a cold Texas morning, while sipping a mug of sekoteng (an Indonesian ginger powder and sugar cane drink I bought in Vietnamese store) and sharing the moment with my adopted mushroom-colored cat and cozy in cookie socks, I found myself reflecting on something simple:
The most valuable thing in recruiting is still human attention.
Technology can help us find candidates. Experience, curiosity, and attentive listening help us understand them.

Thank you to Ma'isya Fathurrohman - and the Maisya Livelihood Network community for demonstrating that meaningful professional connections can be built through trust, genuine understanding, and recognition of people's tangible and intangible assets, rather than through unnecessary questions and assumptions.

posts.text:
I spent last week walking through the facilities of X Origin in Shenzhen, asking one question.

What should a 12-year-old from Singapore, Jakarta or Kuala Lumpur actually learn about robots?

Robotics education for children in China has quietly changed.

It is no longer snapping plastic bricks together to static robot with limited movements.

Robotics and embodied-AI companies are now in the room.
They co-design curricula with education companies.
They set up labs inside schools.
They open their own sites so students can program real robotic arms and watch humanoid robots walk.

Not because the toys got better.
But because children are now learning on the same technology the industry is building.

I see the gap every time I bring overseas students into the Greater Bay Area.

Back home, many robotics classes are still at toy level.
Here, a student watches a robot in action in the morning.
In the afternoon, they write the code that tells it what to do.

Watching a robot and programming one are not the same.
A kit is not a curriculum. It is a toy.

So I am preparing courses for overseas students built around that exposure:

1. Hands-on sessions with real hardware, not only simulations
2. A path that starts with graphical programming for younger students and moves to Python for teenagers
3. Time with engineers, so robotics looks like a career and not just a hobby
4. Facility visits inside our GBA immersion programmes, so students see the whole chain from R&D to the production floor

If you are a parent in ASEAN, are you preparing your child for this, or just signing them up for another toy class?

Imho, young people in ASEAN should not only read about that change.

They should get their hands on it.

Day 63 | 100+ Days Full Stack Developer Challenge 🚀

Moving one step deeper into Advanced Java — today, I completed HTTP Request & Response Handling using Jakarta Servlets.
After learning Servlet fundamentals and lifecycle management, I focused on understanding how browsers communicate with Java applications and how servlets inspect incoming requests and construct appropriate HTTP responses.
The goal was to move beyond theory and implement these concepts through practical programs.

🔹 What I Implemented
I successfully completed 7 practical Servlet programs:
HTTP Request Inspector – Explored request methods, URI, URL, query strings and server information.
HTTP Response Builder – Configured response status, custom headers, content types and character encoding.
HTTP Header Inspector – Examined User-Agent, Accept, Accept-Language, Host, Referer and header enumeration.
HTTP Status Code Handler – Worked with 200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404 and 500 status codes.
Content Type Handler – Generated HTML, JSON and plain-text responses.
Character Encoding Handler – Implemented UTF-8 encoding and multilingual character rendering.
Request Parameter Validator – Handled missing parameters, empty values and multiple parameter values.

🔹 Key Technical Understanding
Two important Servlet components played a central role:
HttpServletRequest – Provides access to incoming request information, headers, parameters and client details.
HttpServletResponse – Helps configure the outgoing response, including status codes, headers, content type and encoding.
Understanding how these two components work together is essential for building Java-based web applications.

Java 21 | Jakarta Servlet | Apache Tomcat 10.1 | Eclipse IDE | HTML5 | CSS3 | HTTP

Day 63 | 100+ Days Full Stack Developer Challenge 🚀

Moving one step deeper into Advanced Java — today, I completed HTTP Request & Response Handling using Jakarta Servlets.
After learning Servlet fundamentals and lifecycle management, I focused on understanding how browsers communicate with Java applications and how servlets inspect incoming requests and construct appropriate HTTP responses.
The goal was to move beyond theory and implement these concepts through practical programs.

🔹 What I Implemented
I successfully completed 7 practical Servlet programs:
HTTP Request Inspector – Explored request methods, URI, URL, query strings and server information.
HTTP Response Builder – Configured response status, custom headers, content types and character encoding.
HTTP Header Inspector – Examined User-Agent, Accept, Accept-Language, Host, Referer and header enumeration.
HTTP Status Code Handler – Worked with 200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404 and 500 status codes.
Content Type Handler – Generated HTML, JSON and plain-text responses.
Character Encoding Handler – Implemented UTF-8 encoding and multilingual character rendering.
Request Parameter Validator – Handled missing parameters, empty values and multiple parameter values.

🔹 Key Technical Understanding
Two important Servlet components played a central role:
HttpServletRequest – Provides access to incoming request information, headers, parameters and client details.
HttpServletResponse – Helps configure the outgoing response, including status codes, headers, content type and encoding.
Understanding how these two components work together is essential for building Java-based web applications.

🔹 Technology Stack
Java 21 | Jakarta Servlet | Apache Tomcat 10.1 | Eclipse IDE | HTML5 | CSS3 | HTTP
📌 Day 63 — Successfully Completed
Seven practical programs, deeper HTTP understanding, and more hands-on experience with server-side Java development.
The journey continues as I strengthen my Advanced Java fundamentals and progress towards Java Full Stack development.
One more day of learning. One more step towards becoming a better engineer.

The AI race won't be won by the smartest model alone. It will be won by whoever can turn intelligence into economic impact at scale.

There is an interesting debate happening in the industry about who is actually leading the AI frontier.

Is it model performance? Intelligence per dollar? Token consumption? Benchmark results?

All are relevant metrics. But I think we're missing a bigger question:

How effectively can we translate frontier AI into real-world economic value?

Looking at Indonesia, the opportunity is particularly interesting.

Consider a few data points:

🇮🇩 AI adoption is accelerating. The latest e-Conomy SEA 2026 report by Google, Temasek and Bain highlights that 54% of Indonesia's working population is already using generative AI.

🇮🇩 The economic opportunity is substantial. Research by Public First estimates that effective AI adoption by Indonesian organizations could contribute Rp620 trillion in economic value by 2030.

🇮🇩 Infrastructure matters. Google's Jakarta Cloud Region has already contributed an estimated Rp900 trillion to Indonesia's economy between 2020 and 2025, according to Public First research.

These numbers tell us something important.

The next phase of AI competition isn't simply about who builds the most intelligent model.

It's about who can bring together five critical capabilities:

1. Frontier intelligence: Building increasingly capable models and AI agents.
2. Infrastructure: Providing the compute, cloud and data foundations to scale.
3. Enterprise data: Connecting AI to trusted, governed and business-critical information.
4. Security and sovereignty: Making AI deployable in highly regulated industries.
5. Ecosystem: Enabling developers, partners and enterprises to innovate together.

This is where I believe Google has a compelling competitive position.

The combination of Gemini, Vertex AI, BigQuery, Google Distributed Cloud and its expanding infrastructure creates an integrated foundation for organizations to move from AI experimentation to enterprise-scale adoption.

And importantly, enterprises don't necessarily want to be locked into one model. They want the flexibility to choose the right intelligence for the right business problem.

For Indonesia, think about banking, telecommunications, manufacturing, healthcare and public services.

The real AI race is no longer just about winning the model race.

It's about building the intelligent economy.

As a UI/UX designer, I never thought I would end up making a game 🎮

This was my very first Game Jam at Apple Developer Academy @ UC, Jakarta. My team and I built When The Light Is Out, a side-scrolling survival horror game set inside a commuter train. The rule is simple: move when the lights are on, stop when they go out. Something is waiting in the dark. 

I worked on the ideation and the art. I drew all the visual assets in Procreate, which I had never opened before this project. I'm used to grids and clean interfaces, so drawing characters and backgrounds by hand felt strange at first. I had to learn it fast, while the deadline kept getting closer.

It ended up being one of the most fun things I've done here. I found out I really enjoy illustrating, and that game design asks the same question I ask in UI/UX every day: how will this feel for the person using it? This time, the answer we wanted was fear.

I also worked closely with the developers, adjusting my drawings quickly so they could keep building. 

Thank you to my team for making this such a good memory. 💜

Vision reads the receipt, an on-device LLM through Foundation Models fixes the messy scan, Nearby Interaction adds friends around you automatically, and CloudKit syncs the bill through iCloud. Basically, there are now zero excuses for pretending you forgot what you ordered. 🧾
